paragraphs: Friend, this is a heavy one, and I won't dress it up. The writer opens by saying that in those days there was "no king in Israel" (Judges 19:1). Then look at who does what. A Levite, a man from the tribe that served God, sends his own concubine out the door to a mob (Judges 19:25). The people of Gibeah, a town in Benjamin, leave a traveler sitting in the square with no one to take him in (Judges 19:15). Nobody in this chapter is doing right.

Here is what I think the passage is teaching. When people stop following God, they don't stay neutral. Things fall apart, and the weakest person pays the most. The Levite is the one who should have known better, and he wants to keep moving even when her father says stay. Then everyone who sees what he sends says, "Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!" (Judges 19:30). I think the writer wants us to stop and take that seriously.

So why does this matter to you, baker? Because you and I do the same thing when we do what feels right to us and leave God out of it. The Bible doesn't skip this chapter, and I think that's because it wants us to see how much we need Him. The story isn't over yet, and neither is the teaching. For now, take this with you: a heart with no king goes wrong, and we need the right King.
